note: What this file is: which painting is which in the lockout shot (lockout-test.js), and how the wet ones were made (21 October 2026, the wet street painter test, round 2; put into the film in log 37), so they can be matched or made again. Both by Flux 3 edit on fal (blackforestlabs/flux-3/edit-image), 2k, then resized to the plate (1536 x 2730), lined up with the kit's align_painting.py and saved as JPEG quality 92 like the files they replaced. The film loads lockout-painted.jpg and lockout-behind.jpg. To go back to the dry street, see 'to_go_back_to_the_dry_street' below.
to_go_back_to_the_dry_street: 1. rename lockout-painted.jpg to lockout-painted-wet.jpg and lockout-painted-dry.jpg to lockout-painted.jpg; do the same for lockout-behind.jpg and lockout-behind-dry.jpg
2. in paper-film/scenes/lockout-test.js, in the look line of pose(), put vignette back to 0.3 and remove toe: 1 (toe 0 is the stage's old curve)
The dry paintings were made in log 29 (lockout-painted-dry.jpg, lockout-behind-dry.jpg; their record is in the project story, log 29). The git history keeps them too.

paintings.prompt: Repaint image 1 completely as a hand-painted illustration in the exact painting style of image 2: the same visible brush strokes, dark ink outlines, simplified painterly textures on brick, stone, slate and wood, and painted wet shine and painted reflections. Nothing should look like a 3D render or a photograph any more. It is a pit-village street at dusk on 1 May 1926, wet after rain. Keep image 1's camera, framing, perspective and every shape, outline, size and position exactly as they are, and keep its pattern of light and dark; change only the brushwork and the colour handling. Keep the small rubbish where image 1 has it (cinders, coal dust, ash, paper scraps, straw, leaves, mud along the gutters and the foot of the walls, round the drum and sacks); add no writing, print or modern litter. Keep: the rusty drum with its open top, dull dark rust-brown, not orange, its top a dark sooty hollow with only a faint orange glow low inside behind the front rim; the dark timber notice board on its two posts with the cream notice (plain paper with grey rows of print-like marks, no readable letters); the small wooden pail at the foot of the board, with no handle; the black gas lamps on their posts down both sides of the street; the brick terraces and stone cottages, the colliery building, its tall chimney and winding wheels; the wooden handcart on the left with its big spoked wheel and the spade leaning on it; the pile of coal sacks in the road; the small heap of black coal lumps on the road; the dustbin at the right edge; and the ladder on the left pavement. The colliery gates are shut: thin dark iron bars across a dim grey doorway whose big doors are closed. Every gas lamp has warm amber glass with a small bright gas mantle inside, and the gas lamp glass glows warm amber. The gutter beside the kerb is a shallow, smooth stone channel with no steps, ridges or grating, with the rainwater lying in it as image 1 shows. The road, pavement and walls are cool blue-grey dusk, and the brick is weathered and greyed by coal smoke without getting any darker. The sky is dark grey-blue cloud with soft edges, like image 2's darker skies; no pale, white or bright clouds anywhere; keep the sky as dark as image 1. The street is wet after rain, and image 1 shows exactly where. Keep all of that wet look exactly where image 1 has it, at the same size and the same strength, painted in the hand of image 2 (painted reflections made of flat shapes of colour with a few ink lines and visible brush strokes; not a photograph, not a mirror): the wet sheen on the setts of the road and on the pavement flags; the lamp, lit-window and brazier reflections lying on the road as soft painted streaks and pools of warm light; the soft reflections of the handcart and the sacks on the road under them; the puddles in the gutters and in the low spots of the road, each one a smooth painted sheet of cool grey-blue with the houses, lamps and lit windows mirrored upside down in it; the thin dark wet lines between the setts and between the flags; and the darker, damper foot of the walls. The road is darker and glossier than a dry road, and never looks dry. Add no wet look where image 1 has none. Keep the thin dark lines between the setts and between the flags everywhere, even where the road shines. Do not make the lamp reflection streaks on the road stronger or longer than in image 1. Warm light stays only where it already is: round the drum, on the board, at the lamps, in the few lit windows, and in their reflections on the wet road where image 1 shows them. Nothing is brighter than the notice. Thin parts (the lamp arms, the gate bars, the cart's rails and spokes, the spade's handle, the winding rope) stay thin and exactly in place, or are left out; never thicken them. Where two things meet or nearly meet, keep each edge exactly where it is and never join them: the drum's side and the board's left post, each gas-lamp head and the wall pipe and bracket beside it, the far lamps and the house downpipes, the spade and the cart's wheel; the winding rope never joins the lamp. Never add: flames, sparks, smoke or steam anywhere (not from the drum, not from any chimney); glows, halos or light rays round any light, the notice or the drum (the wet road's reflections of the lights, and the warm amber of the lamp glass itself, are not halos: keep those as image 1 has them); a handle on the pail; people, animals or birds; extra props (no coal tub, rails, barrel or crates in the road or on the pavement); a moon, stars or any pale, white or bright clouds; new signs or lettering; new or longer shadows.

Thin parts (the lamp arms, the gate bars, the ladder's rails and rungs, the winding rope) stay thin and exactly in place, or are left out; never thicken them. Where two things meet or nearly meet, keep each edge exactly where it is and never join them: each gas-lamp head and the wall pipe and bracket beside it, the far lamps and the house downpipes; the winding rope never joins the lamp.
